title: Emotional Intelligence
authors: Peter Salovey; John D. Mayer
key_findings: First formal framework: EI = set of skills for accurate appraisal and expression of emotion in self and others, effective regulation of emotion in self and others, and use of feelings to motivate, plan and achieve
Places EI inside the older social-intelligence literature
practical_applications: Define EI in any brief as skills (perceive, use, understand, manage), not as a personality label
limitations: Theoretical paper; abstract only read

title: Measuring emotional intelligence with the MSCEIT V2.0
authors: John D. Mayer; Peter Salovey; David R. Caruso; Gill Sitarenios
key_findings: 21 emotion experts and a 2,112-person standardisation sample largely agreed on correct answers, especially where research gives clear answers (e.g., faces)
Reasonable reliability; CFA supported the four-branch model
practical_applications: Ability EI can be tested with right/wrong items; consensus scoring = answers tied to a social group's norms
limitations: Consensus scoring ties 'correct' to the norms of the sample (mostly Western); abstract only

title: Emotional intelligence: New ability or eclectic traits?
authors: John D. Mayer; Peter Salovey; David R. Caruso
key_findings: A schism: some study EI as distinct mental abilities, others an eclectic mix of positive traits (happiness, self-esteem, optimism)
Ability EI shows incremental validity for socially relevant outcomes (authors' claim)
practical_applications: Keep 'EI' for abilities; call optimism/self-esteem by their own names
limitations: Written by the model's originators (interest); this session read the abstract only (author PDF returned 403)

title: The Ability Model of Emotional Intelligence: Principles and Updates
authors: John D. Mayer; David R. Caruso; Peter Salovey
key_findings: Seven guiding principles; reformulated and clarified the four-branch model
Positions EI among other 'hot' intelligences (personal, social)
practical_applications: Use the updated four-branch framing as the studio's working definition
limitations: Abstract only; originators' own update

title: Feeling Smart: The Science of Emotional Intelligence
authors: Daisy Grewal; Peter Salovey
key_findings: Popular and scientific definitions of EI differ sharply; TIME cover asked 'What's your EQ?'
History: social-intelligence speculation, Wechsler 'non-intellective' aspects (1934), Cronbach 1960 'undefined and unmeasured', Gardner 1983 intrapersonal intelligence
Self-report EI overlaps personality (extraversion r=.37 with SREIT vs .11 with MSCEIT, Brackett & Mayer)
Differentiating negative emotions precisely is linked to using more regulation strategies
Self-report vs MSCEIT: bottom quartile overestimates, top quartile underestimates own skill
practical_applications: Granular emotion words in scripts; do not trust self-rated 'I am empathetic'
limitations: Attributes early social intelligence to 'Robert Thorndike ... 1930s', conflicting with Kihlstrom & Cantor (E.L. Thorndike 1920); semi-popular venue; co-author is the model's originator
license: copyrighted (author copy on a U. Miami course page)

title: Social Intelligence (ch. 28 in The Cambridge Handbook of Intelligence)
authors: John F. Kihlstrom; Nancy Cantor
doi_isbn: Cambridge Handbook of Intelligence (R.J. Sternberg & S.B. Kaufman, eds.)
key_findings: Term first used by Dewey (1909) and Lull (1911); modern concept from E.L. Thorndike (1920): 'the ability to understand and manage men and women ... to act wisely in human relations'
George Washington Social Intelligence Test criticised because it correlated highly with abstract intelligence (Thorndike & Stein 1937)
EI (Salovey & Mayer 1990) and social intelligence share a family resemblance but are not the same
PsycInfo titles/abstracts with 'emotional intelligence': 3 before 1990, 77 in 1990s, 1,838 in 2000-2009; popularised by Goleman 1995
practical_applications: History lesson: any 'soft-skill' test must show it is not just IQ or personality
limitations: Scanned chapter; relevant sections read via text extraction

title: Emotional Intelligence: Why It Can Matter More Than IQ
authors: Daniel Goleman
key_findings: Best-seller that popularised EI; secondary sources (Kihlstrom & Cantor 2011; Grewal & Salovey 2005; search summaries incl. Salon 1999) report a TIME cover and a much broader definition incl. zeal and persistence
practical_applications: Cite as cultural history only, not as evidence
limitations: Not read; claims such as 'matters more than IQ' judged overstated by Mayer et al. 2008

title: The Bar-On model of emotional-social intelligence (ESI)
authors: Reuven Bar-On
key_findings: ESI = cross-section of interrelated emotional and social competencies, skills and facilitators; 5 composites (intrapersonal, interpersonal, stress management, adaptability, general mood) and 15 subscales
EQ-i: 133-item self-report; North American norm sample 3,831 (1996); author reports ~4% overlap with cognitive intelligence and ~15% with personality
Author reports average predictive validity .59 across 20 studies
practical_applications: Shows what a 'mixed model' is: optimism, happiness, assertiveness counted as EI
limitations: Most supporting studies are the author's own, some unpublished, mostly cross-sectional; author is the test developer

title: Trait emotional intelligence: psychometric investigation with reference to established trait taxonomies
authors: K.V. Petrides; Adrian Furnham
key_findings: Trait EI = constellation of traits and self-perceived abilities; located as a distinct composite at the primary level of personality hierarchies (Eysenck and Big Five space)
EQ-i was unifactorial in CFA
practical_applications: Trait EI = 'how emotionally capable I think I am' - useful for audience self-image, not skill
limitations: Abstract only

title: Why emotional intelligence is an invalid concept
authors: Edwin A. Locke
key_findings: Argues EI is not a form of intelligence and is defined so broadly it has no intelligible meaning; inadequate when applied to leadership
practical_applications: Use precise sub-skills (perceive, understand, regulate) instead of 'high EQ' as a quality
limitations: Conceptual critique, not data; abstract only

title: Emotional intelligence: An integrative meta-analysis and cascading model
authors: Dana L. Joseph; Daniel A. Newman
key_findings: Cascading model confirmed: emotion perception -> understanding -> regulation -> job performance
Ability EI-performance link inconsistent: positive in high emotional-labour jobs, negative in low emotional-labour jobs
Mixed-based EI explains variance beyond cognitive ability and personality (raises redundancy questions)
practical_applications: EI matters most where the work is emotional labour (service, care, sales) - including writing for emotion
limitations: Abstract only; mixed EI incremental validity may reflect overlap with other constructs

title: The relation between emotional intelligence and job performance: A meta-analysis
authors: Ernest H. O'Boyle Jr.; Ronald H. Humphrey; Jeffrey M. Pollack; Thomas H. Hawver; Paul A. Story
key_findings: Three streams (ability; self/peer report of four-branch; mixed) correlate .24-.30 with job performance (corrected)
Streams 2 and 3 show largest incremental validity beyond IQ and Big Five; publication bias negligible
practical_applications: Effect is real but modest - EI is one predictor among several
limitations: Abstract only; corrected correlations; criteria mostly supervisor ratings

title: Emotional intelligence predicts academic performance: A meta-analysis
authors: Carolyn MacCann; Yixin Jiang; Luke E.R. Brown; Kit S. Double; Micaela Bucich; Amirali Minbashian
key_findings: Overall rho=.20 (N=42,529; k=1,246); ability EI .24 > mixed .19 > self-rated .12
Incremental variance after IQ + Big Five: ability 1.7%, self-rated 0.7%, mixed 2.3%; understanding branch 3.9%, management 3.6%
Ability EI predicts humanities more than science (rho .38 vs .21): emotion understanding overlaps content of literature/history
Perception and facilitation branches add little beyond IQ and personality; reading comprehension may confound ability tests
practical_applications: The branches that matter for creative writing are understanding and managing emotion, not just spotting faces
limitations: Correlational; method overlap; read the accepted manuscript (Oxford repository) discussion

title: A cross-cultural meta-analysis of how leader emotional intelligence influences subordinate task performance and organizational citizenship behavior
authors: Chao Miao; Ronald H. Humphrey; Shanshan Qian
key_findings: Leader EI shows incremental validity for subordinate task performance and OCB after Big Five and cognitive ability
Link stronger in collectivistic, feminine, high uncertainty-avoidance cultures; OCB link also stronger in high power-distance cultures
practical_applications: In hierarchical, collectivist settings the senior person's emotional skill may matter more
limitations: Country-level Hofstede scores as moderators (ecological); read abstract and highlights of the accepted manuscript

title: Empathy and Its Discontents
authors: Paul Bloom
key_findings: (As described by Vastfjall et al. 2017) Empathy is a poor moral guide: spotlights single identified individuals, favours the in-group, can motivate harmful acts; prefers compassion and cost-benefit reasoning
practical_applications: Do not equate 'more empathy' with 'more ethical' messaging
limitations: Abstract not available (publisher elided); content known only via the commentary and book summaries

title: Against Empathy: The Case for Rational Compassion
authors: Paul Bloom
key_findings: (Search summaries) Emotional empathy as a 'spotlight' on individuals here and now; argues for rational compassion; mixed reception (e.g., Greater Good review says the case falls short)
practical_applications: Pair emotional single-character stories with honest scale/context
limitations: Book not read

title: Commentary: Empathy and its discontents
authors: Daniel Vastfjall; Arvid Erlandsson; Paul Slovic; Gustav Tinghog
key_findings: Bloom's 'compassion' is ill-defined; identifiable-victim and singularity effects track a drop in compassion, not only empathy; compassion is also biased
Both empathy and compassion are poor guides without deliberation; design institutions that channel emotion toward moral values
practical_applications: Emotion + structure: an emotional story should still be accurate about the size of a problem
limitations: Short commentary

title: Empathy: A motivated account
authors: Jamil Zaki
key_findings: Empathy is both automatic and context dependent; motives drive approach or avoidance
Avoid motives: suffering, material costs, interference with competition; approach motives: positive affect, affiliation, social desirability
People regulate empathy via situation selection, attentional modulation and appraisal
practical_applications: Audiences avoid content that only shows suffering with nothing to do; give an approach motive (affiliation, a doable action)
limitations: Abstract only

title: Empathy: A review of the concept
authors: Benjamin M.P. Cuff; Sarah J. Brown; Laura Taylor; Douglas J. Howat
key_findings: 43 definitions reviewed; 8 themes incl. cognitive vs affective, congruent vs incongruent, self/other distinction, trait vs state, automatic vs controlled
practical_applications: Name which empathy a brief needs: understanding (cognitive) vs feeling-with (affective)
limitations: This session read the abstract (registry already lists full text)

title: On the universality and cultural specificity of emotion recognition: A meta-analysis
authors: Hillary Anger Elfenbein; Nalini Ambady
key_findings: Emotions recognised across cultures above chance, with an in-group advantage (higher accuracy within same national/ethnic/regional group)
Advantage smaller with more contact; majority members poorer at judging minority members than the reverse
practical_applications: Thai audiences read Thai expression best; foreign viewers may miss subtle cues - test with real viewers
limitations: Mostly posed expressions; abstract only

title: Emotion Regulation: Current Status and Future Prospects
authors: James J. Gross
key_findings: Process model: different strategies have different consequences
Extended process model: regulation as valuation with three stages - identification, selection, implementation
practical_applications: Comfort dialogue can target each stage: notice the feeling, choose a strategy, try it
limitations: Abstract only

title: Individual differences in two emotion regulation processes: Implications for affect, relationships, and well-being
authors: James J. Gross; Oliver P. John
key_findings: Habitual reappraisers experience/express more positive and less negative emotion and have better interpersonal functioning; habitual suppressors the reverse
practical_applications: Characters who model reappraisal rather than 'just hold it in'
limitations: Correlational, US samples; abstract only

title: Dealing with feeling: A meta-analysis of the effectiveness of strategies derived from the process model of emotion regulation
authors: Thomas L. Webb; Eleanor Miles; Paschal Sheeran
key_findings: 306 experimental comparisons: attentional deployment d=0.00 overall; response modulation d=0.16; cognitive change d=0.36
Distraction works (d=.27); concentrating on the feeling does not (d=-.26)
Suppressing expression d=.32, but suppressing experience or thoughts does not work (-.04, -.12)
Reappraising the stimulus (.36) or perspective taking beats reappraising the response (.23)
practical_applications: 'Look at it from her side' (perspective taking) is a stronger story turn than 'stop thinking about it'
limitations: Lab inductions, short-term outcomes; abstract only

title: Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being
authors: Richard M. Ryan; Edward L. Deci
key_findings: Three innate needs - competence, autonomy, relatedness - when satisfied yield self-motivation and mental health; when thwarted, diminished motivation and well-being
practical_applications: Encouraging messages should give choice (autonomy), a doable step (competence) and company (relatedness)
limitations: Abstract only this session

title: Positive Self-Statements: Power for Some, Peril for Others
authors: Joanne V. Wood; W.Q. Elaine Perunovic; John W. Lee
key_findings: Low self-esteem participants who repeated 'I'm a lovable person' felt worse than those who did not; high self-esteem participants felt better, to a limited degree
Focusing on how the statement was both true and not true helped low self-esteem people more than focusing only on how it was true
practical_applications: Avoid blanket affirmations for audiences who doubt themselves; use believable, partial, specific reassurance
limitations: Small student samples; replication status not checked this session; abstract only

title: Exploring compassion: A meta-analysis of the association between self-compassion and psychopathology
authors: Angus MacBeth; Andrew Gumley
key_findings: 20 samples / 14 studies (all Neff Self-Compassion Scale): r=-0.54 between self-compassion and psychopathology (depression, anxiety, stress)
Significant heterogeneity; no evidence of publication bias
practical_applications: Self-kindness framing ('it is human to be tired') is a defensible tone for comfort content
limitations: Correlational; overlap of the scale with negative affect debated; abstract read from the Glasgow eprint

title: A Meta-Analysis of Interventions to Reduce Loneliness
authors: Christopher M. Masi; Hsi-Yuan Chen; Louise C. Hawkley; John T. Cacioppo
key_findings: Randomised studies: pooled effect -0.198 (small); pre-post and non-randomised designs inflate effects
Among randomised studies, interventions addressing maladaptive social cognition were most effective (vs social skills, support, access)
practical_applications: Stories about loneliness can gently challenge the thought 'nobody wants me', not only say 'go out more'
limitations: Few studies per category; English-only 1970-2009; read first part of PMC full text

title: Loneliness and Social Isolation as Risk Factors for Mortality: A Meta-Analytic Review
authors: Julianne Holt-Lunstad; Timothy B. Smith; Mark Baker; Tyler Harris; David Stephenson
key_findings: Adjusted OR for mortality: social isolation 1.29, loneliness 1.26, living alone 1.32; objective and subjective isolation similar
Comparable with well-established mortality risk factors
practical_applications: Loneliness is a serious topic: handle with care, not as a joke or a sales hook
limitations: Observational; confounding possible; abstract only

title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Social Media Exposure to Upward Comparison Targets on Self-Evaluations and Emotions
authors: Carly McComb; Eric J. Vanman; Stephanie J. Tobin
key_findings: 48 articles, 7,679 participants, 118 effects: upward comparison on social media lowers self-evaluations/emotions g=-0.24
Body image g=-0.31, subjective well-being -0.19, mental health -0.21, self-esteem -0.21; contrast is the dominant response
practical_applications: Comparison-themed stories should not themselves become a highlight reel; show the hidden backstage
limitations: Short-term experimental exposure; abstract only (full text 403)

title: Effects of feedback intervention on performance: A historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory
authors: Avraham N. Kluger; Angelo DeNisi
key_findings: 607 effect sizes: feedback improves performance on average d=.41, but over one third of feedback interventions decreased performance
Effectiveness drops as feedback moves attention away from the task toward the self
practical_applications: Critique the work, not the person; say what to change on the task
limitations: Abstract only

title: The Power of Feedback
authors: John Hattie; Helen Timperley
key_findings: Feedback is a major influence on learning but can be positive or negative depending on type and delivery; proposes a model of properties and circumstances that make it effective
practical_applications: Feedback should answer where the work is going, how it is going, and what next
limitations: Educational context; abstract only this session (registry lists full text)

title: A Review and Meta-Analysis of Person-Centered Messages and Social Support Outcomes
authors: Andrew C. High; James Price Dillard
key_findings: 23 studies: positive linear association between person-centeredness of support messages and actual effectiveness; stronger for perceived effectiveness
Association attenuated in confederate-based methods; the nine-level hierarchy needs clearer measurement
practical_applications: Comforting lines should acknowledge, legitimise and explore the other's feeling rather than deny or fix it
limitations: Abstract only; vignette-heavy literature

title: Hierarchy, 'Kreng Jai' and Feedback: A Grounded Theory Study Exploring Perspectives of Clinical Faculty and Medical Students in Thailand
authors: Rosawan S. Areemit; Christine M. Cooper; Kunthida Wirasorn; Pope Paopongsawan; Chaiyapon Panthongviriyakul; Subha Ramani
key_findings: Thai hierarchy perpetuates one-way top-down feedback; kreng jai (balance between consideration for others and self-interest) affects feedback seeking and giving; seeking feedback seen as a burden on teachers
Students accept harsh feedback when it includes suggestions; feedback is most credible when the giver knows the student's effort
practical_applications: In Thai feedback scenes the junior rarely asks; the senior must open the door; pair critique with a concrete fix
limitations: One medical school, qualitative; abstract via Europe PMC

title: Criticism in the Workplace: A Sociopragmatic Analysis (in Thai)
authors: Sirawat Thaithae
doi_isbn: Journal of Liberal Arts, Thammasat University 26(1)
key_findings: 60 Thai public/private employees, discourse completion test with 4 scenarios: three strategies - opting out, direct, indirect criticism
Face-to-face: more opting out or indirect than behind-the-back; direct criticism mostly toward juniors; with bosses, seniors and peers people avoid or go indirect
Formality, future interests and presence of high-status people increase avoidance or mitigation
practical_applications: Thai feedback scenes: indirect criticism is the norm with seniors; directness toward juniors signals status
limitations: Small sample, hypothetical scenarios; abstract read from the PDF

title: Understanding Organizational Practice Adoption at the Thai Subsidiary Corporation
authors: Tim G. Andrews; Nartnalin Chompusri
key_findings: Kreng jai shapes how a Thai subsidiary adopts e-communication, performance appraisal and empowerment; it sometimes supports, extends and sometimes contradicts etic cultural-dimension predictions
practical_applications: Do not reduce Thai behaviour to one Hofstede score; kreng jai is situational
limitations: Qualitative single case; abstract via RePEc

title: The Anatomy of Thai Face
authors: Larry S. Persons
key_findings: Ethnography: five constructs form Thai 'face' - na-ta, kiat, saksi, chuesiang, barami - distinct though not mutually exclusive, with a dynamic model
practical_applications: 'Face' in Thai stories is several things (look, honour, dignity, reputation, moral authority) - name which one is at stake
limitations: Single-author ethnography; abstract read

title: Psychology of the Thai People: Values and Behavioral Patterns
authors: Suntaree Komin
key_findings: (Search summaries) Nine Thai value clusters ordered by importance, led by ego orientation and grateful-relationship orientation, then interdependence, fun-pleasure, achievement-task; survey of ~2,469 Thais 1978-81 (blog-reported)
practical_applications: Background for Thai character motives (face/ego, bunkhun gratitude)
limitations: Not read; date inconsistent (1990/1991); sample figure from a blog

title: Preventing suicide: a resource for media professionals, update 2023
authors: World Health Organization; International Association for Suicide Prevention
key_findings: Fourth edition; includes digital/social media; imitation risk rises with extensive, sensational, method-describing or normalising coverage and myths; growing evidence that survival/resilience stories are protective

Dos: accurate help information, educate with facts, report coping/recovery stories, care with celebrity suicides and bereaved, staff well-being; Don'ts: prominent placement, method/location detail, sensational language, single-cause explanations, images, suicide notes
practical_applications: Studio rule: no method, no location, no 'it solved the problem', add help line, show coping
limitations: Full PDF not retrieved (403/404); read the WHO launch page and HKU CSRP's summary of the Dos and Don'ts

title: Role of media reports in completed and prevented suicide: Werther v. Papageno effects
authors: Thomas Niederkrotenthaler; Martin Voracek; Arno Herberth; Benedikt Till; Markus Strauss; et al.
key_findings: 497 Austrian print reports: repetitive reporting of the same suicide and suicide myths associated with higher suicide rates
Coverage of suicidal ideation without suicidal behaviour, and 'mastery of crisis' stories (coping without suicide), associated with lower rates (Papageno effect)
practical_applications: Stories of getting through a dark period, with coping shown, are the protective format
limitations: Ecological, one country, six months; abstract only

title: Association between suicide reporting in the media and suicide: systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Thomas Niederkrotenthaler; Marlies Braun; Jane Pirkis; Benedikt Till; Steven Stack; et al.
key_findings: Celebrity suicide reports: suicide risk +13% (RR 1.13) over 1-2 months; when method reported, same-method deaths +30% (RR 1.30)
General suicide reporting: no clear association (RR 1.002)
High heterogeneity, some publication bias; responsible-reporting guidelines are the best available population-level intervention
practical_applications: Never depict or name a method; real-case or celebrity references need extra care
limitations: Observational designs; fictional portrayals excluded; read PMC full text (first 100k chars)

title: Association of Logic's hip hop song '1-800-273-8255' with Lifeline calls and suicides in the United States: interrupted time series analysis
authors: Thomas Niederkrotenthaler; Ulrich S. Tran; Madelyn Gould; Mark Sinyor; Steven Sumner; et al.
key_findings: In 34 days after the three peaks of public attention, Lifeline received ~9,915 excess calls (+6.9%) and suicides were ~245 (5.5%) below expected
practical_applications: A creative work centred on help-seeking and hope can be associated with protective outcomes
limitations: Time-series association, not proof of causation; abstract only

title: Association Between the Release of Netflix's 13 Reasons Why and Suicide Rates in the United States: An Interrupted Time Series Analysis
authors: Jeffrey A. Bridge; Joel B. Greenhouse; Donna Ruch; Jack Stevens; John Ackerman; et al.
key_findings: Suicide rate in US 10-17-year-olds rose after release (IRR 1.29), driven by boys (1.35); no significant change for adults; homicide control unchanged
Estimated ~195 additional youth suicides Apr-Dec 2017; authors: caution with youth exposure, 'no discernible public health benefit'
practical_applications: Fiction is not exempt from safe messaging; graphic depiction aimed at youth is the documented failure
limitations: Quasi-experimental; cannot separate content from promotion; read PMC full text

title: Newspaper Reporting of Suicides in Thailand: Compliance with WHO Media Guidelines
authors: Manote Lotrakul; P. Suwannakan
doi_isbn: Journal of the Psychiatric Association of Thailand 67(2):203-211
key_findings: 309 reports in Thairath, Dailynews, Khaosod (Jan-Jun 2019): ~98.7% described method and location, ~90% named the victim, ~44% front page, ~40% sensational headlines, ~29% victim images; only ~4% gave help-seeking information
practical_applications: Thai news style is far from WHO guidance - never copy it for suicide-adjacent content
limitations: Three papers, six months; abstract page read

title: The Ethics of Manipulation (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
authors: Robert Noggle (author as listed by SEP; name not shown in fetched text)
doi_isbn: SEP, first published 30 Mar 2018; substantive revision 31 Mar 2026
key_findings: Accounts: bypassing/undermining reason, trickery (inducing faulty beliefs/emotions), non-coercive pressure, hybrids; Noggle's mistake account
Emotional appeals are not necessarily manipulative (e.g., graphic smoking warnings, Golden Rule appeals)
No consensus on which nudges/framings are manipulative; manipulation usually seen as pro tanto wrong (harm, autonomy, treating persons as things)
practical_applications: Test: does the emotion fit the facts, and would the viewer endorse the influence if they saw how it works?
limitations: Read ~100k of 119k characters; author attribution not confirmed in fetched text

title: Dark Patterns at Scale: Findings from a Crawl of 11K Shopping Websites
authors: Arunesh Mathur; Gunes Acar; Michael J. Friedman; Elena Lucherini; Jonathan Mayer; Marshini Chetty; Arvind Narayanan
key_findings: ~53K product pages from ~11K shopping sites: 1,818 dark-pattern instances, 15 types in 7 categories; 183 sites used deceptive practices; 22 third parties sell dark patterns as a turnkey service
practical_applications: Fake urgency/scarcity and confirmshaming are emotional manipulation - banned in studio copy
limitations: Abstract only

title: Experimental evidence of massive-scale emotional contagion through social networks
authors: Adam D.I. Kramer; Jamie E. Guillory; Jeffrey T. Hancock
key_findings: Reducing positive posts in News Feeds led users to post fewer positive and more negative words, and vice versa
practical_applications: Feeds transmit mood; a studio's tone choices add up across many viewers
limitations: Effect sizes very small; consent controversy (see Verma2014); abstract this session

title: Editorial Expression of Concern: Experimental evidence of massive-scale emotional contagion through social networks
authors: Inder M. Verma
key_findings: PNAS editor concerned the Facebook experiment may not have fully met informed-consent and opt-out principles; Cornell IRB deemed it outside its program because Facebook ran it for internal purposes
practical_applications: Testing emotional effects on real audiences needs consent-like care; never A/B test distressing content
limitations: Editorial; read PMC full text

title: Unsung Hero (Thai Life Insurance, Ogilvy & Mather Bangkok) - Cannes Lions case and press coverage
authors: Thai Life Insurance; Ogilvy & Mather Bangkok (director Thanonchai Sornsriwichai per The Drum)
key_findings: (Search summaries of Cannes Lions case, Selfstorming, The Drum) >10M views in two weeks, ~17M in a month across 232 countries; later 110M+ views; sparked 'try not to cry' reaction videos
practical_applications: Kindness-without-reward story, brand only at the end
limitations: Case page did not render; view figures are secondary and vary by date; no sales/effect data

title: Dove: Real Beauty Sketches (Cannes Creative Effectiveness Gold) - WARC case summary
authors: Unilever (agency not shown in fetched page)
key_findings: FBI-trained sketch artist drew women from their own and from strangers' descriptions; film claimed as the most-watched online film; Gold, Creative Effectiveness Lions, 15 June 2014
practical_applications: Self-perception gap made visible; also a lesson in critique (critics called it self-esteem marketing)
limitations: Brand-side award summary; no independent figures; criticism known only via search summaries (Business Insider 2013, CBC)

title: Pepsi pulls widely mocked ad featuring Kendall Jenner (AP via ABC13)
authors: Associated Press / ABC13
key_findings: Ad showed Jenner handing a Pepsi to a police officer at a smiling protest; critics said it trivialised protest and evoked the Ieshia Evans photograph; Pepsi defended it on Tuesday and pulled it on Wednesday: 'Clearly we missed the mark, and we apologize'
practical_applications: Borrowing a real collective pain for a feel-good brand moment = emotional appropriation
limitations: News report
